questions.q: What does a qubit's T1 value, as reported in a calibration report, actually represent?
options: The exact physical temperature of the dilution refrigerator at the time of calibration
The number of times the qubit has been used in prior experiments
The total number of gates that can be applied before the qubit must be replaced
Roughly how long the qubit holds an excited state before decaying (energy relaxation time), usually reported in microseconds
questions.explain: T1 is the energy relaxation time -- roughly how long a qubit typically holds an excited state before decaying -- and is one of the core per-qubit fields in a calibration report, usually in microseconds.

questions.q: Why do two-qubit gate (edge) error rates vary noticeably between different connections on the same chip?
options: Edge error rates only depend on how many total qubits the chip has, not on which specific pair is used
Edge error rates are randomly assigned by the provider's software and have no physical basis

A chip is not uniform -- different physical qubit pairs and their connecting hardware have different real-world performance, so error rates can span more than a factor of two between the best and worst edges on the same device
Every connection on a chip always has an identical error rate by design
questions.explain: Real chips are non-uniform: specific qubit pairs and their physical coupling vary in performance, so two-qubit gate error rates can differ substantially from one edge to another even on the same device.

questions.q: A circuit has high gate depth and a total expected runtime that approaches a meaningful fraction of a candidate qubit's T2 time. What should this prompt a practitioner to do?
options: Favor qubits with longer coherence times for this circuit, since decoherence is likely to show up directly in the results as circuit runtime approaches T2
Reduce the number of shots submitted, since that is the only factor T2 affects
Assume the result will be unaffected, since T2 only matters during qubit idle time, not during active circuits
Ignore T2 entirely, since it only matters for single-qubit gates
questions.explain: When a circuit's total gate time approaches a qubit's coherence time, decoherence becomes a real, direct contributor to error -- favoring qubits with longer T1/T2 for deeper circuits is a practical mitigation.

questions.q: Why is a device's 'last-calibrated' timestamp useful when deciding whether to trust its published numbers right now?
options: The timestamp has no practical use beyond historical record-keeping

Comparing the timestamp's age against that platform's typical drift behavior helps judge whether the calibration data is still likely to reflect current performance, rather than assuming it's permanently accurate
A newer timestamp always means the device is currently degraded
The timestamp guarantees the device will perform identically to its calibration data for exactly 24 hours afterward
questions.explain: Since qubit parameters drift, an older calibration timestamp (relative to that platform's typical drift rate) is a signal the published numbers may be less reliable right now -- there's no single universal freshness rule, since drift rates vary by platform.

questions.q: Why might a device with a very good median error rate still be unsuitable for a specific circuit?
options: Median error rates are never actually calculated by providers, only estimated by users
The median number doesn't guarantee enough simultaneously good qubits and edges, arranged in the specific connectivity pattern the circuit actually needs
A good median error rate always guarantees every individual qubit and edge is equally good
Median error rate only applies to readout error, never to gate error
questions.explain: A device can have strong overall statistics while still lacking a sufficient cluster of good qubits and edges in the exact pattern a given circuit requires -- which is why checking per-qubit and per-edge data for your specific circuit matters more than the median alone.
